Target Keyword: multiple pages ranking for same keyword
Associated Keywords: keyword cannibalization, content cannibalization, same keyword multiple pages, keyword cannibalization fix
Friction: The standard advice for multiple pages ranking for the same keyword is merge-and-301, written as if every competing page deserves saving. Nobody publishes the actual cost in impressions and clicks, so site owners either panic-merge pages with genuinely distinct intents or leave twenty pages splitting signals for years. We have the numbers: four cannibalized clusters on our own site, twenty pages, and a clean same-domain control group.
Logic: Lead with the measured cost: seven pages aimed at one intent pulled 2,318 impressions and 2 clicks over three months, none reaching the top 15 — while four new pages with distinct intents on the same weak domain reached positions 17-32 within four days. Mechanism: the engine must pick one candidate per query; more candidates means no page accumulates enough signal, and internal links dilute across the set. The contrarian step the standard advice skips: before merging, ask whether the cluster serves an abandoned strategy — consolidating pages you should retire is optimizing waste. Give the five-minute overlap check (pull top 10 for both queries, count shared URLs, more than half means one query) and the three-way decision: differentiate, consolidate, or retire.
content_angle: A cannibalization postmortem measured on our own Search Console: twenty pages across four clusters, page-by-page impressions and positions published, plus a same-domain control group that isolates the mechanism. Names the decision the merge-advice genre skips — whether the competing pages should exist at all — and is honest that our own case ended in retirement questions, not consolidation wins.
